clue.text: Hope left here for a lesser temple

definitions.text: Hope left here for a lesser temple

parts.words: Hope left here for a lesser temple
parts.note: David Hope, Archbishop of York, stepped down in 2005 to become a humble parish priest, leaving his great cathedral for a smaller church

explanation.surface: Hope departs a grand place of worship for a humbler one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hope' reads as the abstract virtue, as in Dante's 'abandon hope', but it is the churchman David Hope, who left the see of York for a parish in Ilkley.
explanation.definitionFit: The cathedral church of the Archbishop of York is the great Gothic building he left behind.

clue.text: "I say! You, a Macbeth forsaken? O, rubbish!" (Lady M on his appearance)

indicators.note: rubbish means the preceding words are nonsense to be thrown together and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in mock horror at Macbeth being deserted, with a stage note about his wife's remark on his looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubbish' signals that all the quoted words from 'I say' to 'O' are rearranged; the parenthesis is the definition, pointing to Lady Macbeth's line in Act 1 Scene 5 warning her husband that his expression betrays him.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare gives Lady Macbeth this line telling her husband his countenance can be read openly, a comment on his appearance.

clue.text: Black bottom outside giving concrete support

indicators.note: outside means the word for bottom sits around the letter for black

parts.note: bottom means rear, the backside
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A dance called the Black Bottom somehow props up a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black bottom' looks like the 1920s dance, but the words split: B for black goes inside REAR for bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel reinforcing bar is set inside concrete to strengthen it, a support for the structure.

clue.text: Making Bunthorne declaim: "I would hear this!"

parts.note: Bunthorne is the setter's pseudonym, so it means me
to declaim is to rant, speak loudly and pompously
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter, who shares his name with the posturing poet in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, is invited to orate and someone wants to listen.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter refers to himself, and 'declaim' gives RANT. The definition is a pun: 'would hear this' is to be heard as 'wood here, this', pointing to a timber.
explanation.definitionFit: A pun: say 'would hear' and you get 'wood here'; this is a hardwood timber from South-East Asian trees.

clue.text: Sudanese hairstyle turned up on Scotsmen

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means the word for a hairstyle is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a bun is a hairstyle with the hair coiled at the back of the head
Ian is a typically Scottish name, so Ians are Scotsmen

explanation.surface: A Sudanese hairdo is worn by men from Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Nubians are people of Nubia, a region straddling southern Egypt and northern Sudan, so Sudanese people.

clue.text: Killing hybrid rose in the fourth dimension

indicators.note: in means the shuffled flower goes inside the word for the fourth dimension

parts.note: time is often called the fourth dimension after length, breadth and height

indicators.note: a hybrid is a cross, so the letters of rose are mixed into a new form

explanation.surface: A hybrid rose bred over time somehow proves deadly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hybrid' gives RESO from the flower's letters. 'Killing' looks like murder, but it is the colloquial sense of exhausting, as in a killing schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing in the informal sense of exhausting or wearisome matches something tedious and draining.

clue.text: At which the odds are five to one against a hole in one

definitions.text: At which the odds are five to one against a hole in one

parts.words: At which the odds are five to one against a hole in one
parts.note: reads like golf betting odds on an ace, but the hole is a bullet wound in the head from a revolver with one loaded chamber of six

explanation.surface: Bookmakers quote the odds against a golfer holing in one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hole in one' suggests golf; it means a bullet hole in the one player, and with one live round in six chambers the odds are five to one against.
explanation.definitionFit: This deadly game has one bullet in a six-chamber revolver, giving five-to-one odds against being shot.

clue.text: Surprise! A cuff below the belt aimed at turf accountancy

parts.note: a turn-up is the folded cuff at the bottom of a trouser leg, well below the belt
aimed at means for, intended for
a turf accountant is a bookmaker

explanation.surface: A low punch thrown during a dispute over betting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cuff below the belt' sounds like an illegal punch in boxing; it is a trouser turn-up. 'Turf accountant' is a jokey British name for a bookmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an unexpected outcome, something that would astonish even the bookmakers.

clue.text: Indian outfit abandoned a marsh walk before the incoming Dutch sea

indicators.note: abandoned means let loose, wild, so these letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: incoming in a down clue means coming up, so the Dutch word is read upwards

parts.note: zee is the Dutch word for sea

explanation.surface: Someone gives up a walk across a marsh before the North Sea tide comes in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' rearranges A MARSH WALK into SHALWARKAM; 'incoming' turns ZEE to EEZ.
explanation.definitionFit: This loose trouser-and-tunic combination is a traditional dress of South Asia, worn in India and Pakistan.

clue.text: Most of the Roman town crier's ultimate American wit

indicators.note: most of means all but the final letter of the word the

parts.note: urbe is Latin for in the city, from urbs, the Roman word for a town

indicators.note: ultimate means the last letter of the word crier's, ignoring the possessive

explanation.surface: A town crier in ancient Rome turns out to be an American humorist.
explanation.walkthrough: TH (the, cut short) plus Latin URBE plus R, the end of 'crier's'.
explanation.definitionFit: James Thurber was an American humorist and cartoonist known for his New Yorker pieces.

clue.text: Abort school meals for East Europeans in here

indicators.note: in here points to the letters that sit inside the run of words just given

explanation.surface: A school cancels its meals for children from Eastern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'aBORT SCHool'.
explanation.definitionFit: This beetroot soup is a staple dish of Russia, Ukraine and Poland.

clue.text: Concerning France, before and possibly after the votes

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
F is the international vehicle code for France
ere is a poetic word for before

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of and might be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A remark about France holding polls before and maybe after something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' gives NDA from the letters of the conjunction; 'after' simply places that last.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular votes on a single question are plebiscites, and this is the Latin-style plural.

clue.text: Leak from a lighter

definitions.meaning: a leak is an escape of liquid, an accidental overflow
a thin strip of wood or twisted paper used to light a fire or pipe

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an accidental release of liquid and a taper used for lighting fires.

clue.text: Fearsome Scottish soldier who won stripes from university

parts.note: a non-commissioned officer, a corporal or sergeant, wears chevron stripes earned by promotion

explanation.surface: A frightening Highland soldier earned his rank after leaving university.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldier comes 'from university', so U leads. The answer is a Scots word for strange or uncanny.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect this adjective means strange, uncanny, eerie, hence fearsome.

clue.text: Craving to soak Huxley's palliative in a mix

parts.note: to dip something is to soak it in liquid
soma is the happiness drug in Aldous Huxley's novel Brave New World

indicators.note: mix means the letters of in a are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A craving to steep the drug from Brave New World in some mixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craving to soak' looks like the whole definition, as the answer is a craving for drink, but only 'Craving' defines. 'a mix' turns IN A into NIA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an uncontrollable craving for alcohol, a morbid compulsion to drink.

clue.text: Successful potter here made richer

definitions.meaning: in snooker or pool, a ball potted successfully ends up inside a table pocket
having gained money from a deal, ahead financially

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both where a snooker ball goes when potted and an idiom for having made a profit.

clue.text: Iron skirts? Time, I see, to be demanding women's rights

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
minis are miniskirts
taken as written
the letter C is pronounced the same as see

explanation.surface: Someone ironing miniskirts decides it is time to campaign for equality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron' looks like a verb about pressing clothes, but it is the element.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for advocating the equality of the sexes, so campaigning for women's rights.

clue.text: Operatically secret smoker giving up when entering a year in Rome

indicators.note: giving up in a down clue means the assembled word is turned to read upwards
entering means the word for when goes inside the Latin year

parts.note: annus is Latin, the language of ancient Rome, for year
as means when, as in as I left

explanation.surface: A secret smoker gives up the habit when a new Roman year begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving up' looks like quitting smoking; it turns the whole container upwards, giving ANNASUS read in reverse. In Wolf-Ferrari's opera Il segreto di Susanna a wife hides her smoking.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Wolf-Ferrari's one-act opera hides her cigarette habit from her husband.

clue.text: One's company sustaining one dramatist

indicators.note: sustaining means holding up from below, so in a down clue the rest sits beneath the single letter

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written, the possessive spelt out

explanation.surface: A theatre company keeps one playwright going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sustaining' puts ONESCO under I in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Ionesco was a Romanian-French playwright of the Theatre of the Absurd.

clue.text: See 1 down & 7
Expression of relativity from artist to Spanish relative

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
tio is Spanish for uncle

explanation.surface: An artist writes to his Spanish uncle about Einstein's theory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relativity' suggests Einstein; it means comparing quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: A proportion of one quantity to another expresses their relative sizes.

clue.text: With which insects feel sick in awful UN mess

indicators.note: in means the word for sick goes inside the jumbled letters
awful means the letters of UN mess are in a dreadful jumble

parts.note: ill means sick

explanation.surface: Insects feel sick at the terrible mess left by the United Nations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges UN MESS into SENSUM, and ILL goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensillum is a small sense organ, such as a hair or bristle, by which an insect perceives touch or taste.

clue.text: See 1 down
Lend an ear to Livingstone!

parts.note: to lend an ear to someone is to hear them
Ken Livingstone was the Mayor of London

explanation.surface: An appeal to listen to the politician Ken Livingstone.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both defines a word for listening and builds it; Ken Livingstone was London's first elected mayor.
explanation.definitionFit: To lend an ear is an idiom for listening attentively, an archaic verb with the same sense.

clue.text: Insomniac screened here in Washington

parts.note: the 1993 romantic film Sleepless in ..., about a widower who cannot sleep, is set in a city in Washington State

explanation.surface: An insomniac is screened somewhere in the US capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washington' suggests the capital city, but it is Washington State; 'screened' points to the film Sleepless in Seattle.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest city of Washington State gave its name to the film about a sleepless widower.

clue.text: Poleaxe tart? Mad project!

indicators.note: mad means crazed, so the letters of the two words go wild and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A deranged plan to fell a pastry with a battleaxe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' rearranges POLEAXE TART.
explanation.definitionFit: To project is to estimate future values by extending a known trend, the same as inferring beyond the data.
